feedback: If the chart shows it: 'Look how the warm marks bunch up in summer and the cold ones in winter — your own chart shows the pattern.'
'You noticed it gets dark much earlier in winter — that's the short winter days showing up in your observations.'
activities.intendedInsight: The seasonal pattern is something you can SEE accumulate in your own recorded observations, not just be told about. Day length is a concrete, chartable observation.
learnerActions: Over the year, add a mark to a shared weather/temperature chart for the weather you observe locally.
Each season, compare your own trees, clothes and daylight to what you recorded.
Look back over the chart to spot the seasonal rhythm building up as real data.
Note when it gets dark across the year and compare summer with winter.
activities.title: Build a year-long weather chart

feedback: If a learner picks summer for shortest days: 'Think about how late it stays light in summer — summer has the LONGEST days; winter has the shortest.'
If the order is wrong after autumn: 'After autumn comes winter, then spring again — try turning the wheel in your head.'
activities.intendedInsight: A confirmation step, best used AFTER the hands-on wheel/chart work, to check whether naming, ordering, weather-matching and day-length targets have stuck. It checks the pattern but does not by itself make the child produce or explain the cycle.
learnerActions: Put the four seasons in order, and say what comes after autumn.
Match each season to its typical weather.
Answer: which season has the shortest days? Which has the longest?
activities.title: Order and match check (after the hands-on work)
